title: The Secret Garden
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
openingText: Everyone said that Mary Lennox was the most disagreeable-looking child they had ever seen. They said it when she was sent to Misselthwaite Manor to live with her uncle, and it was true. She had a thin little face and a thin little body, with thin, light hair and a sour look. Her hair was yellow, and so was her face, because she had been born in India and had always been sick with one thing or another. Her father had worked for the English Government and had always been busy and unwell himself. Her mother had been a great beauty who cared only about going to parties and having fun with cheerful people. She had not wanted a little girl at all. When Mary was born, she handed her over to an Ayah, who was made to understand that if she wanted to please the Mem Sahib, she must keep the child out of sight as much as she could. So when Mary was a sickly, fussy, ugly baby, she was kept out of the way. When she grew into a sickly, fussy toddler, she was kept out of the way too. The only faces she ever remembered seeing every day were the dark faces of her Ayah and the other native servants. They always obeyed her and let her have her own way in everything, because the Mem Sahib would be angry if her crying disturbed her. So by the time Mary was six years old, she was as bossy and selfish a little pig as ever lived. The young English governess who came to teach her to read and write disliked her so much that she quit after three months. When other governesses came to fill the job, they always left even sooner than the first. So if Mary had not decided that she really wanted to learn to read books, she would never have learned her letters at all. One terribly hot morning, when she was about nine years old, she woke up feeling very cross. She became even crosser when she saw that the servant standing by her bed was not her Ayah. “Why did you come?” she said to the strange woman. “I won’t let you stay. Send my Ayah to me.”
about:
Frances Hodgson Burnett (1849–1924) published The Secret Garden in 1911. Mary Lennox, a sour and neglected child, is sent from India to her uncle’s great house on the Yorkshire moor. There she finds a garden that has been locked for ten years, a servant boy who understands animals, and a hidden cousin who believes he is dying.

The book follows the garden’s return to life and the children’s with it. This edition keeps Burnett’s story and voice in clear modern English.

whyItMatters.title: A book about neglect and recovery
whyItMatters.body: Mary and Colin begin as sick, angry and unloved. The story shows, step by step, how air, work, friends and attention change them. It is a good book to discuss with a young reader.

whyItMatters.title: Nature written with attention
whyItMatters.body: Burnett describes seeds, weather, birds and soil with close care. The moor and the garden are almost characters. Readers who garden will recognize the details.

whyItMatters.title: Class and voice
whyItMatters.body: Mary’s upbringing, Martha’s Yorkshire speech and Colin’s household show how class shaped childhood in Edwardian England. The way each child talks tells you where they come from.

angleCards.title: Watch Mary change
angleCards.text: Mark where Mary first acts kindly or curiously. What causes each change?
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Secret Garden to follow how Mary changes.

angleCards.title: Colin’s illness
angleCards.text: Note what Colin believes about himself and what changes his mind.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Secret Garden to understand Colin’s illness and recovery.

angleCards.title: The garden itself
angleCards.text: Track each stage of the garden’s year and what each one means for the children.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Secret Garden to read the garden as a symbol of recovery.

angleCards.title: Voices and class
angleCards.text: Listen to how Martha, Dickon, Ben Weatherstaff and Mrs. Medlock speak, and what that says about them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Secret Garden to see how speech shows class and character.
